title: Kamsa's death

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kamsa's death began: a sleepless king, an elephant at the gate, and one boy in the arena seen many ways, and by Kamsa, as death. What did you bring into a room yesterday? Day nine hundred six.

The women in the stands are not happy. Down on the wrestling ground, Kamsa's champion Chanura has squared off against Krishna, and his partner Mushtika against Balarama. Grown men built like mountains, against two boys from the cow pastures. The Bhagavata lets us hear the crowd: this is wrong, the women say to one another. It's no fair match. Whoever allowed it shares the blame. And they say the cowherd girls of Vraja were lucky, to see him every day. Today, the end of the fight, and the end of this part of the story.
screen: `CHANURA AND MUSHTIKA.` → `TWO BOYS AGAINST GIANTS.` → `THE CROWD SAYS, THIS IS WRONG.`

segments.voice: The fight goes hold for hold, and then it turns. Krishna brings down Chanura, Balarama brings down Mushtika, and the other wrestlers fall or run. The arena erupts. Kamsa, on his high platform, orders the music stopped. He shouts for the two boys to be driven out of the city, for the cowherds' goods to be seized and Nanda arrested, for Krishna's father Vasudeva and his own father Ugrasena to be killed. Before he finishes, Krishna is on the platform. Kamsa reaches for his sword. Krishna catches him by the hair, pulls him down into the arena, and it's over. Then the Bhagavata says something that's hard to forget. All his life, Kamsa thought of Krishna. Eating, drinking, walking, sleeping, he thought of nothing else, out of fear. And because his mind was so fixed on him, the text says, he reached him in the end. It's the same frame we heard at the rasa lila: what matters is where the mind is turned, even if it's turned there by terror. The story doesn't end only in triumph. Kamsa's wives come weeping, and Krishna comforts them and sees that the funeral rites are done. Then he goes to free his parents, Vasudeva and Devaki, whom Kamsa had put in chains again. He frees them and bows at their feet. And so this part closes where it began. The birth in a prison cell. The crossing of the Yamuna in the storm. Putana, the butter thief, the mouth full of the universe. Kaliya, Govardhan, the flute, the dance in the moonlight, the road out of Vrindavan. And now the cell door open, and a son kneeling in front of his mother.
screen: `THE WRESTLERS FALL.` · `HE WAS NEVER NOT THINKING OF HIM.` · `KAMSA'S WIVES ARE COMFORTED.` · then, large: `THE PRISON DOOR OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Kamsa spent his life running from what he feared, and the fear kept Krishna in his mind anyway. For these two minutes, bring to mind one small fear you've been carrying. Not the biggest one. Let it sit in front of you, and look at it plainly: its shape, its size, where you feel it in your body. Don't argue with it, and don't run. Breathe with it until it's simply there. Then, if you like, picture a door opening somewhere you've been shut in. If you pray, you can hold that fear before God, or before Krishna, for one breath. The bell holds the time.
Kamsa's death. The king who spent his life afraid of Krishna, pulled down in his own arena, and reaching him, the text says, through his fear.
Your line: the prison door opens. Today, when an old fear comes back, look straight at it for one breath instead of running from it. Day nine hundred six.

howItsDone: Kamsa's death and the freeing of Devaki and Vasudeva are retold from the Bhagavata, and Kamsa's defeat is acted out in festival performances in the Mathura area.

notes: End of the part 'Bhagavata Purana — Krishna's childhood' (days 879–906): the teach names the part's stories in order.

All paraphrase. Confirm against Bhagavata 10.44: Chanura vs Krishna and Mushtika vs Balarama; the women's protest that the match is unfair and their praise of Vraja's women; Kamsa's orders (stop the music, expel the cowherds, seize Nanda's wealth, kill Vasudeva and Ugrasena); Krishna seizing him by the hair; the verse that Kamsa, thinking of him in fear while eating, drinking, moving and sleeping, attained him; consoling Kamsa's wives and the funeral rites; freeing Vasudeva and Devaki.
Kamsa had released Vasudeva and Devaki after the birth (10.4) and chained them again after Narada's visit (10.36); the script says 'in chains again', confirm.
The text (10.44–45) adds that Vasudeva and Devaki at first held back, knowing him as God, and that Ugrasena was restored as king; left out for length.
howItsDone refers to festival performances of Kamsa's defeat in the Mathura area (Kamsa Vadh); confirm or cut.

Editor pass: Kamsa's orders corrected (drive out the two boys, seize the cowherds' goods, arrest Nanda); 'doesn't end in triumph' softened since the text has celebration; practice and carry rewritten because 'notice where your mind keeps returning' repeated day 900; howItsDone de-duplicated.
Audit: 'the match is short' cut; 10.44 describes the wrestling at some length, hold by hold, before Chanura and Mushtika fall.
